title: Don't Confuse Nostalgia With Good Teaching
author: Kara Andy
summary: Kara Andy rejects false binaries in education (screens vs. paper, old vs. new, AI vs. learning) in favor of intentional, balanced design. Neither pencil nor Chromebook is automatically rigorous; the question is whether learning is well-designed. Eighty-minute lectures lose students as much as passive screen time; good teaching requires students to think, discuss, create, revise, and reflect. AI can strengthen teacher capacity by generating differentiated texts, checks for understanding, and station materials, freeing teachers to lead discussion and conferences. Schools should fight for better instructional design (not panic), teacher training (not bans), clear AI guardrails (not avoidance), and balanced tool use (not digital overload). Students need both deep reading and research tools, both handwriting and collaborative spaces—responsive classrooms know when to use each.
points: False binaries (screens vs. paper, traditional vs. innovative) miss the real issue: instructional design and intentionality matter far more than the tool itself.
An 80-minute lecture is no more rigorous than passive screen time; both can lose students. Good teaching requires thinking, discussing, creating, and reflecting regardless of tools.
AI can remove friction (generating differentiated texts, formative checks, station materials) so teachers spend more time where they matter most: discussion, feedback, relationships.

Schools should fight for purposeful technology use based on learning goals, not blanket bans or overload; sometimes handwriting helps memory, sometimes a Chromebook opens doors neither can replace the other.
Clear AI guardrails (transparency, ethical use, verification habits) build AI literacy better than avoidance, because students are already encountering AI and need guidance.
quotes: An 80-minute lecture does not become rigorous just because there is no screen involved.
Good teaching has never been about the tool alone. It has always been about the design.
Students do not need less opportunity to think, create, revise, collaborate, and access support. They need better-designed learning experiences.
Thoughtful use is balanced use. It is not about filling every moment with a device. It is about making choices that deepen learning, increase access, and create more room for great teaching.
A balanced classroom is not confused. It is intentional.” Archived from Brewing Innovation on April 21, 2026 by Tim.
